<explanation>
Based on your provided file structure and README, this project is the Ruby on Rails application that powers the OpenStreetMap website and its API. The system is, in effect, a full-stack web application that handles everything from user accounts, diary entries, messaging, an API for XML/JSON-based editing, an integrated iD editor, browsing of map data, and GPX uploads. Here’s how to sketch and document the system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the main components of the system:
   • Application Server: This is the Rails application itself. In your diagram, show the “Rails Application” box that internally has layers for controllers, models, views (the typical MVC structure) as well as jobs and services.
   • API Layer: Depict a distinct API module/component that handles the XML/JSON requests (see folder “app/controllers/api” and the various jbuilder view templates for JSON and XML).
   • Frontend & Integrated Editor: Since the project includes the integrated version of the iD editor and browse pages, clearly indicate a “Frontend” or “Web UI” component (representing the views, assets in “app/assets”, and public code in “public/”).
   • Database: As a PostgreSQL-dependant Rails application, show the “Database (PostgreSQL)” with connections to Rails (including ActiveRecord models under “app/models”). You might also note that there are migrations and a “db” folder that define data schema and indexes.
   • External Services: The documentation and README state that a full installation depends on external map tile servers and geocoding services. Draw external boxes for “Map Tile Server”, “Geocoding Services”, and possibly “OAuth Provider” (given the presence of oauth2 controllers and tables) and “Translation Service” (via Translatewiki).
   • Background Processing: Visualize a component for asynchronous and scheduled tasks (e.g., delayed jobs or ActiveJob – see the jobs directory in “app/jobs”) for tasks like trace importing/destroying.
   • Auxiliary Components: Optionally, illustrate parts like the integrated GPX processing (see lib/gpx.rb and the API endpoints under “app/controllers/api”) and any support libraries used (e.g., for rate limiting or geolocation).

2. Determine relationships and interactions:
   • The Rails Application sits in the middle. Draw arrows between the “Web UI” (frontend) and the “Rails Application” to represent user interactions.
   • Show the API endpoints interfacing with external requests (via the “api” controllers) and the client applications.
   • Draw bidirectional arrows between the Rails Application and the PostgreSQL Database, emphasizing CRUD operations and the role of ActiveRecord.
   • Illustrate external integrations by drawing arrows from the Rails Application to “Map Tile Server” and “Geocoding Service” (highlighting outgoing API calls, e.g., for rendering maps or geocoding addresses).
   • Represent background jobs and asynchronous processing as part of the Rails system that interacts with the database and external systems.

3. Highlight important architectural patterns and design principles:
   • MVC Pattern: Clearly indicate the separation of concerns between Models (data and business logic), Views (presentation), and Controllers (request handling).
   • RESTful API: Emphasize that many parts of the system expose RESTful endpoints (API v0.6) and that the routing (config/routes.rb) organizes these resources.
   • Modular and Component-Based Design: Within the Rails app, several subdomains exist – user accounts (controllers/accounts, models/user, mailers), messaging (controllers/messages, user_mailer), GPX handling, and map browsing. Each of these can be viewed as a self-contained module in your diagram.
   • Integration with third-party services: Visualize external dependencies on map tile servers and geocoding services, marking them distinctly.
   • Background Job Processing: Indicate that jobs like trace_importer_job and trace_destroyer_job function asynchronously.

4. List relevant technologies and frameworks:
   • Ruby on Rails, PostgreSQL, and the use of standard Rails libraries/frameworks.
   • Various dependencies (from Gemfile); you might mention libraries related to OAuth2, i18n, error handling, file uploads (ActiveStorage), background job processing, etc.
   • Docker and Vagrant files hint at containerized development and provisioning strategies, so you might also include deployment/infrastructure layers if that helps your audience.

5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram:
   • For this full-stack web application, separate clearly the frontend (views, assets, public folder) from the backend (controllers, models, API endpoints).
   • Indicate the separation between the user interface (for website browsing, editing with the embedded iD editor) and the API layer that supports programmatic interactions.
   • Identify integration points with external services (tile servers, geocoding) and note that these are not part of the core repository but are crucial for a full-function installation.

6. Elements to include in the diagram:
   • Component boxes: Label each part—“Rails App,” “API Layer,” “Web UI,” “Database (PostgreSQL),” “External Map Tile Server,” “External Geocoding Service,” “Background Job Processor.”
   • Directional arrows: Use arrows to show data flows:
       – From user browsers to the Web UI and then to the Rails Application.
       – Between the Rails App and Database (bidirectional).
       – From Rails App to external services (outgoing requests).
       – From background jobs back to the Database or external notifications.
   • Use color coding or different shapes: For example, choose one shape or color for internal components (Rails app internals) and another for external integrations.
   • Notations for frameworks/technology stacks attached to each component (e.g., “Ruby on Rails” on the Rails App, “PostgreSQL” on the Database, “Docker/Vagrant” on the deployment layer if desired).

7. Final advice:
   Pay attention to the level of detail needed. You do not have to map every controller or migration; rather, break the system down into high-level modules that capture all the major functions (user management, diary entries, messaging, maps/editing API, GPX processing). A detailed layered diagram emphasizing separation of concerns will best convey the architecture. Use clear labels, directional data flow arrows, and consistent color coding or shapes to make the overall design easy to follow at a glance.

This approach will give you an accurate system design diagram that tailors your explanation specifically to the openstreetmap-website project. It captures both the internal Rails architecture and its interactions with various external services that together support the website and API functions.

Happy diagramming!
</explanation>
